--- title: "Masterarbeit" author: "Luca Leon Happel" date: "2026-01-21 14:00" categories: - math - algebra - topology - category theory - Deutsch image: "./assets/universal_covering.png" format: html: code-fold: true lightbox: match: auto effect: fade desc-position: bottom loop: true --- I was writing my masters thesis about the connection between a generalization of the reidemeister-torsion (called $\ell^2$-alexander torsion) and the [thurston norm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thurston_norm) of 3-manifolds. Check it out, if you like: [Masterarbeit.pdf](/masterarbeit) Some pictures of it can be found [here](https://www.instagram.com/stories/highlights/18097883624515441/). ## How To Read This Thesis In contrast to traditional thesis, I have extensively used hyperlinks to make it easier to read. Specifically section 4 (the main part of the thesis) relies heavily on the results of section 1 to 3. This made the main part of the thesis only around 25% of the total length, while the introductory sections are around 75%. However, the thesis heavily relied on hyperlinks. Expanding these in section 4 inflates it massively and shows its true length. My idea was to make the main proofs as concise as possible, by relying on all the previous results and definitions extensively. (In dark mode the hyperlinks are highlighted in a light blue color, so they are easier to spot. In light mode they also work, but they are not highlighted, as my supervisor wanted) ::: {layout-ncol=3} ![Let us look at lemma 4.24 which proofs the main theorem for manifolds whose JSJ-decomposition contains a hyperbolic part. In the proof, we can just click to where the JSJ-decomposition is defined.](./assets/highlighted-links.png){.lightbox group="how-to-read"} ![After clicking on "JSJ-Zerlegung", the definition is shown. We are also shown directly what hyperbolic parts are. We also have directly above a few examples (3d-renders) of how such an incompressible torus of the JSJ-decomposition might look like (here a seifert part).](./assets/following-links.png){.lightbox group="how-to-read"} ![When clicking on "incompressible", we also have directly the definition together with a visualization of it.](./assets/following-links2.png){.lightbox group="how-to-read"} ![The definition of "incompressible" however used "proper embedding" internally, which is also reachable by hyperlink and visualized.](./assets/following-links3.png){.lightbox group="how-to-read"} ![Next up in the proof, "hyperbolic" is used. We can follow this definition twice, until it is completely unfolded.](./assets/following-links4.png){.lightbox group="how-to-read"} ![Skipping towards the end of the proof, we can find "quasi fibered classes" being used. We can follow this (1) to its definition, where these are defined as limits of "fibered classes", which we can again look up (2). I have defined them in a non-standard way (equivalent to the standard definition, but I found my way more intuitive) and I provided examples for them (3) and counterexamples as well (4).](./assets/following-links5.png){.lightbox group="how-to-read"} ::: In general I strive to convey the _semantics_ more than just the _syntax_. During this thesis, this was very hard and juggling mathematical correctness with intuitive explanations. I tried to use a more modern approach an used hyperlinks, which might be non-standard. I am certain that this kind of format will become the future of how we write and read mathematical texts though, as hyperlinks and visualizations are a no-brainer for conveying complicated ideas. ## Critique My thesis was criticized, and the main points of critique boil down to the following points: 1. The visualizations are not rigorous enough (possibly childish) 2. Some examples (like the "physical interpretation") of reidemeister torsion and its applications to physics were redundant 3. The notation is non-standard 4. The main part (section 4) is disproportionally short (only 25%) compared to the introductory sections (75%) 5. I had a mistake in definition 2.22 where I stated the absolute reidemeister torsion is independent of the choice of representation 6. It seemed rushed Here are my thoughts on these points: 1. The main ctiricism was that I used 3d renders of a car in a tube which I have twisted using blenders geometry nodes to visualize "what life is like" in a seifert manifold: ::: {layout-ncol=3} ![3d renders of a car in a tube](./assets/thesis-car.png){.lightbox} ::: However, I was inspired by classical textbooks like "William L. Burke, Applied Differential Geometry (Cambridge University Press, 1985).", which had this visualization (also including a car): and also [Conway's classical ZIP proof](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/francisweeks.pdf) of the classification of surfaces, which uses pants and zippers to visualize the core ideas from geometry and topology: ::: {layout-ncol=3} ![William L. Burke, Applied Differential Geometry (Cambridge University Press, 1985), pp 44](../../assets/assets/burke-car.png){.lightbox group="various-visualizations"} ![Conways zip proof](../../assets/assets/conway-zip.png){.lightbox group="various-visualizations"} ![George K. Francis, A Topological Picturebook, 2007](./assets/topological-picture-book.png){.lightbox group="various-visualizations"} ![George K. Francis, A Topological Picturebook, 2007](./assets/topologicalpicturebook2.png){.lightbox group="various-visualizations"} ![I was told my visualizations should have been more technical, like this visualization of a triangulation of a surface from "Holger Kammeyer, Introduction to Algebraic Topology (Springer International Publishing, 2022)"](../../assets/assets/kammeyer-simplicial.png){.lightbox group="various-visualizations"} ::: 2. Regarding the physical interpretation, and general references to physics/cosmology, I think that there should be no shame in that. Physics and mathematics go hand in hand and I think it is cool to actually find applications of pure mathematics in "real like" (aka. physics). Also, I was quite proud of my "physical interpretation" of reidemeister torsion, as it related the predecessor of $\ell^2$-alexander torsion (reidemeister torsion) to electromagnetism. In fact, to see this connection one has to walk a fun journey through algebra, geometry, topology and analysis. I also just really liked how the geometric series suddenly showed up and related to monopoles and answered the question of "what does the reidemeister torsion actually measure?" ::: {layout-ncol=3} ![A short except from the passage about physical interpretations](../../assets/assets/electro-magnetism.png) ::: 3. Fair enough, I used $\lll$ and $\ggg$ instead of $\lambda$ and $\rho$ for the left and right regular representation. I still think regarding currying that this was the right choice. It also more closely aligns with how group actions are usually denoted as $a \triangleright x$ for $a \in G$ and $x \in X$ with $G \curvearrowright X$. ::: {layout-ncol=3} ![Left and right actions using "weird" notation](../../assets/assets/rrr.png){.lightbox group="group-action"} ![On wikipedia, group actions are also denoted using more "triangular" shapes](../../assets/assets/action.png){.lightbox group="group-action"} ::: 4. The main section being short has already been explain in "How To Read This Thesis" above. 5. I have indeed stated an incorrect theorem. I have fixed that mistake since. The reidemeister torsion is only independent of the choice of representation _up to equivalent_ representations. This was clear in my submitted thesis, but I nontheless made it more explicit now. This error feels more like when students forget to say "up to isomorphism" in their proofs. 6. Yes, I did have various grammatical and spelling errors. Also, the bibliography (exported using [Zotero](https://www.zotero.org/)) had mistakes in it, which I did not catch. Should have been more careful and proofread it more often. From this I have learned that I should have asked my supervisor more often for feedback, as errors could have been caught earlier. Regarding the visualizations and examples from physics, I still like them. Also the modern hyperlink based approach I would not like to change; but it seems the mathematical community is not ready for it yet. ## Analyzing My Progress I reuse some code i have from [my post where I analyze my NixOS GitHub repository](/posts/nixos-git-analysis/). ::: {#8a79f4fe .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import os from datetime import date, datetime import git REPO_URL = "https://github.com/quoteme/masterarbeit.git" REPO_DIR = "/tmp/quoteme-masterarbeit" CUTOFF_DATE = date(2025, 10, 8) repo : git.Repo = ( git.Repo(REPO_DIR) if os.path.exists(REPO_DIR) else git.Repo.clone_from(REPO_URL, REPO_DIR, bare=True) ) repo.remotes.origin.fetch("+refs/heads/*:refs/heads/*") commits = [ commit for commit in repo.iter_commits('--all') if commit.committed_datetime.date() >= CUTOFF_DATE ] if not commits: raise ValueError(f"No commits found on or after {CUTOFF_DATE.isoformat()}") # summary of the total number of commits print(f"Total commits: {len(commits)}") print(f"First commit: {datetime.fromtimestamp(commits[-1].committed_date)}") print(f"Last commit: {datetime.fromtimestamp(commits[0].committed_date)}") print(f"Avg. time between commits: {(commits[0].committed_date - commits[-1].committed_date) / len(commits) / 3600:.2f} hours") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Total commits: 405 First commit: 2025-10-08 10:56:26 Last commit: 2026-10-12 15:32:45 Avg. time between commits: 21.88 hours ``` ::: ::: ::: {#c390b271 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} import plotly.graph_objects as go commits_sorted = sorted(commits, key=lambda c: c.committed_datetime) commit_dates = [c.committed_datetime for c in commits_sorted] commit_indices = list(range(1, len(commits_sorted) + 1)) fig = go.Figure( data=[ go.Scatter( x=commit_dates, y=commit_indices, mode="markers", marker=dict(size=7, color="#4C78A8", opacity=0.85), hovertemplate="Date: %{x|%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S}
Commit #: %{y}", showlegend=False, ) ] ) fig.update_layout( title=f"Commits since {CUTOFF_DATE.isoformat()} · quoteme/masterarbeit", xaxis_title="Date", yaxis_title="Commit number", template="plotly_white", height=450, ) fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: {#2cf1049d .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} from collections import Counter from datetime import timedelta import numpy as np import plotly.graph_objects as go forecast_end_date = date(2026, 4, 6) daily_counter = Counter(c.committed_datetime.date() for c in commits_sorted) observed_end_date = max(daily_counter.keys()) observed_dates = [ CUTOFF_DATE + timedelta(days=i) for i in range((observed_end_date - CUTOFF_DATE).days + 1) ] observed_daily = np.array([daily_counter.get(d, 0) for d in observed_dates], dtype=float) observed_cumulative = np.cumsum(observed_daily) t_obs = np.arange(len(observed_dates), dtype=float) slope, intercept = np.polyfit(t_obs, observed_cumulative, deg=1) all_dates = [ CUTOFF_DATE + timedelta(days=i) for i in range((forecast_end_date - CUTOFF_DATE).days + 1) ] t_all = np.arange(len(all_dates), dtype=float) linear_cumulative = np.clip(slope * t_all + intercept, a_min=0.0, a_max=None) # Plot 1: linear model forecast linear_fig = go.Figure() linear_fig.add_trace( go.Scatter( x=observed_dates, y=observed_cumulative, mode="lines+markers", name="Observed cumulative", marker=dict(size=5), line=dict(width=2), ) ) linear_fig.add_trace( go.Scatter( x=all_dates, y=linear_cumulative, mode="lines", name="Linear regression", line=dict(width=2, dash="dash"), ) ) linear_fig.add_vline( x=observed_end_date, line_width=1, line_dash="dash", line_color="gray", ) linear_fig.update_layout( title=f"Linear model extrapolation until {forecast_end_date.isoformat()}", xaxis_title="Date", yaxis_title="Cumulative commits since cutoff", template="plotly_white", height=460, ) linear_fig.show() expected_linear = float(linear_cumulative[-1]) print(f"Expected cumulative commits by {forecast_end_date.isoformat()} (linear): {expected_linear:.1f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Expected cumulative commits by 2026-04-06 (linear): 235.6 ``` ::: ::: # Conclusion From the commit graph one can clearly see that I have spent the first 3 months researching and not writing. Once I got the hang of the topic, I started writing, spending pretty much every wake hour on it and submitting the thesis on time. If I were to do it again, I would however start writing earlier, even while still doing research, so that in the end I have more time to polish the thesis and request feedback from my supervisors.
